body: Welcome to the third edition of The Accountant for this year, which brings together a wealth of information relevant to our profession and provides an overview of the work and initiatives the Institute has been involved in over the past few months.

I would like to take this opportunity to reflect on some of the issues that, in my view, underline the relevance of the Institute and the contribution we can make. Indeed, the relevance of an Institute is not measured only by the number of events it organises or the number of consultations it responds to, even though the numbers are quite impressive. However, I believe relevance is also measured by the Institute's ability to be present when important issues are being discussed, to understand the challenges faced by its members and to bring the collective experience of the profession to the table.

Through our engagement with Government, regulators, public authorities and other local and international stakeholders, the Institute has continued to make sure that the voice of its members is heard where decisions affecting accountants and the wider economy are being considered.

Our meeting with the National Audit Office (NAO) earlier this summer was particularly meaningful in this regard. It gave us an opportunity to better understand the needs of accountants working within the NAO and, more broadly, those working in the public sector. It was also a reminder of the breadth of our membership and of our responsibility to represent accountants, regardless of where they work.

Our participation in the Malta Tax and Customs Administration Stakeholder Panel that was established this summer provided another important channel through which the Institute could contribute to discussions on taxation and policy. We also met with Minister for Finance Clyde Caruana following his re-election, discussing continued collaboration and issues affecting the profession, including those emanating from international policy positions.

These engagements are valuable not only because they give us the opportunity to put forward the views of accountants, but also because they enable us to listen. Representation should never be one-directional. Understanding the challenges faced by others is essential if we are to contribute constructively to policy discussions.
This is particularly true in taxation.

As we do every year, the Institute is engaging with members and different stakeholders as part of the preparation of its proposals for the forthcoming Budget. Through this process, we can draw on the experience of the profession and put forward recommendations that we believe can contribute to a stronger and more effective tax framework.

At the same time, the work of the Institute does not begin and end with the Budget. Some matters require more immediate attention, while others are better addressed through policy or administrative changes. In such cases, the Institute will continue to engage directly with the relevant authorities.

This is part of what I believe a modern professional institute should do: not simply react to decisions once they have been made but contribute to the conversation early enough to help shape better outcomes. That role is becoming increasingly important as the environment in which accountants operate becomes more complex. Regulation continues to evolve, artificial intelligence is changing the way professional services are delivered and expectations of accountants and auditors continue to expand.
In this environment, maintaining trust in the profession is essential.

Accountants are trusted with information that is fundamental to businesses, investors, public authorities and individuals. That trust carries responsibilities. It requires professional competence and sound professional judgement, independence, integrity and a willingness to uphold standards even when doing so is not the easiest option.
I also believe the profession has a wider responsibility to society.

Financial literacy is one area where accountants can make a meaningful contribution. We work with financial information every day, but our knowledge can also help individuals, families and businesses better understand financial decisions, risks and opportunities. I recently participated in a televised discussion on financial literacy, and I believe this is an area where the profession can have a much broader impact too.
Our standing as a profession will ultimately depend not only on what we do within our workplaces, but also on how we contribute to the communities and economy around us.

This is also why I believe the Institute must remain open to different perspectives. We need strong relationships with Government and regulators, but we must also engage with business, academia and other professional bodies. We may not always agree, but constructive dialogue is essential.

Added to this, I also look forward to seeing more members contributing and participating in the Institute’s events. From now until the end of the year, there is certainly no shortage of opportunities for us to meet, learn and contribute. Our programme includes a range of social and technical events, CPE sessions and other initiatives, and I encourage all members to take an active part in them. The strength of the Institute comes from the involvement of its members, from sharing knowledge and experience to engaging in the discussions that shape our profession. I hope to see many of you at our upcoming events, to exchange ideas, strengthen our connections and most importantly, continue building an Institute that remains relevant to all of us.

Welcome to another edition of our flagship publication, The Accountant. I hope the summer months have given you an opportunity to recharge and return refreshed ahead of another busy period for the profession and for the Institute.

As we enter the final quarter of the year, the Institute’s work continues across a wide range of areas, from technical and policy matters to professional development and member engagement. For this edition of The Accountant, I would like to share with you a few updates on some of the work currently underway, particularly how we are strengthening the way the Institute draws on the expertise and experience of its members.

We are currently working with the Institute’s different working groups to discuss their priorities and define the areas where their contribution can have the greatest impact. This is important because the Institute’s work is strongest when it is informed by the practical experience of members working across the different areas of the profession. By bringing together this expertise, we can ensure that our engagement is relevant, informed and focused on the issues that matter most.

This collaborative approach is reflected in the Institute’s ongoing, proactive and solutions-based engagement with authorities and other stakeholders. By way of example, recent discussions have included engagement with Malta Enterprise in relation to MicroInvest, and with the Malta Business Registry and the Malta Tax and Customs Administration on liquidations. Through these discussions, the Institute seeks to balance the needs of the authorities with the practical realities and professional responsibilities of accountants and auditors, ensuring that requirements are workable and aligned with professional expectations and standards. At the same time, the Institute supports professionals through the necessary guidance, helping to establish clear expectations on both sides and enhance consistency in reporting and implementation.

Our contribution to the fight against money-laundering and the upcoming National Risk Assessment is another example of this engagement. As Malta prepares for its next wave of assessments, first through its national exercise and eventually through the next MONEYVAL evaluation, the Institute has an important role to play in the national discussion. Our feedback to the National Coordinating Committee has focused on assessing data, the identification and mitigation of risks, and the respective roles and responsibilities of accountants and auditors. This work is particularly important given the role that professionals across our sector play in maintaining strong systems and standards that support the integrity of Malta’s financial services industry.

At the same time, digitalisation continues to cut across virtually every area of the profession. This is reflected in the way the Institute has positioned its Digitalisation Group as a horizontal group, recognising that technology cannot be considered separately from financial reporting, audit, taxation, professional skills or the wider delivery of professional services.

The Group is supporting initiatives such as the Professional Accountants in Business (PAIB) Conference and continues to engage with various stakeholders to explore opportunities that may support the profession’s digital transformation. For accountants, digitalisation is not simply about adopting new tools or technologies. It also raises important questions around professional judgement, ethics, data, skills and how the role of the professional will evolve.

That same focus on the future brings us to another area that requires our attention: talent. Ensuring that accountancy remains attractive to the next generation is essential to the continued strength and relevance of our profession.

Over the past couple of years, we have gathered significant insight into how accountancy can remain attractive to the next generation. We have now reached a pivotal point at which we need to assess our available resources, prioritise our next steps and determine where our efforts can have the greatest impact, whether among students, educators, parents, practising accountants or a combination of these groups. We are also working with the University of Malta on an event for first-year students in the year ahead, as part of our broader efforts to communicate the opportunities offered by the profession more effectively.

Importantly, we do not have to address this challenge in isolation. We are pairing our local efforts with strong international engagement, which continues to provide valuable opportunities to exchange ideas and learn from the experiences of others.

An important initiative by the International Federation of Accountants is bringing professional accountancy organisations together to strengthen the profession’s appeal and relevance. The initiative provides a global platform for sharing research, practical resources and successful approaches to attracting and retaining talent, while developing a more consistent narrative about the opportunities and wider value of a career in accountancy. The Institute’s participation provides a platform to collaborate with international counterparts, share experience and draw on these global insights and resources. By working together, we can develop a stronger, more consistent message that can be adapted effectively to Malta’s needs.

This international cooperation was also reflected in a visit from our Lithuanian counterparts together with representatives from their university. While our respective professional environments and structures are not necessarily identical, the visit highlighted the value of peer-to-peer collaboration and the exchange of perspectives.

The visit offered an excellent platform for mutual knowledge sharing. It allowed us to exchange experience on shared priorities, including stakeholder areas such as engagement, regulatory cooperation and the links between the profession and collaboration with academia. Relationships such as these are valuable because they enable us to look beyond our own environment and consider how different approaches can inform our continued development.

All of this work provides an important backdrop to what promises to be a particularly active final quarter of the year. We will be resuming our highly successful Meet the Regulator series, giving members an opportunity for direct engagement and discussion with key regulatory authorities. These sessions are an important part of the Institute’s commitment to creating meaningful channels of dialogue between members and those responsible for regulation.

An event being led by the PAIB Group, under the theme The Future of Finance Leadership, will bring together Chief Financial Officers (CFOs), Chief Executive Officers and other industry experts, to explore how the role of the finance leader is evolving. Discussions will cover artificial intelligence and integrated thinking, sustainability and resilience, today’s business challenges and the ethical dilemmas facing CFOs and Boards. November will then bring about our annual Tax Conference, having become an established and important element of the Institute’s calendar and a valuable opportunity for members to discuss the latest developments in taxation.

Alongside our professional activities, we remain committed to supporting the wider community. We are particularly proud of our increased collaboration with the Malta Trust Foundation, and I encourage members to keep the 29th of November free for a day of football, padel and other activities in support of this important cause. Stay tuned to our socials for more information on this special event which will combine networking with a rewarding social and charitable cause.

I therefore encourage members to continue engaging with the Institute, our groups and the many activities taking place over the coming months. The stronger that connection is, the better placed we are to represent the profession, support our members and ensure that accountancy continues to evolve while retaining the standards, values and professional judgement on which it has always been built.

The Malta Institute of Accountants’ (MIA) Senior Technical Officer, Veronica Micallef, attended the Audit and Assurance Policy Group Meeting organised by Accountancy Europe. The meeting focused on key European Union (EU) audit policy developments, with particular attention given to proposals aimed at simplifying audit requirements for smaller entities while preserving audit quality and stakeholder confidence. Discussions also covered differing interpretations of group audits and common control arrangements, anti-money laundering-related developments and the ongoing review of the Public Interest Entity framework. A significant portion of the meeting was dedicated to International Standard on Auditing 540, where participants debated whether the standard should be revised or supported through additional guidance, highlighting the need for proportionality, scalability and practical implementation. Broader discussions addressed audit quality indicators, regulatory convergence, common supervision methodologies and ongoing initiatives by the European Commission and the Committee of European Auditing Oversight Bodies, with a shared emphasis on achieving greater efficiency and consistency across the European audit landscape.

MIA Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Maria Cauchi Delia participated in Accountancy Europe’s Members’ Assembly in Brussels, joining representatives of member bodies from across Europe to exchange views on the strategic direction and future of the accountancy profession. The discussions focused on the profession’s role in supporting sustainable growth, small and medium-sized enterprises access to liquidity and a more competitive European business environment. Members considered the progress of Accountancy Europe’s Purpose 2030 initiative, current EU policy and regulatory developments and emerging risks and opportunities arising from growing assurance demands, regulatory simplification, new market entrants and technological change. The programme also featured exchanges on the future of the profession and on developments in sustainability reporting, including the need for regulatory stability and proportionate implementation. Through its active participation in Accountancy Europe, the MIA continues to contribute Malta’s perspective to European discussions, remain closely informed of developments affecting the profession and strengthen its collaboration with counterpart bodies. This engagement supports the Institute’s work in anticipating change, informing its policy positions and helping members navigate an evolving professional and regulatory landscape.

MIA President Dr Jonathan Dingli appeared on Net TV’s Flusek, a programme sponsored by FinanceMalta as part of a series promoting financial literacy. The appearance forms part of the MIA’s ongoing commitment to promoting financial literacy and supporting greater public understanding of financial and business matters. During the interview, Dr Dingli discussed the core elements of company financial statements and how they provide a clear overview of a company’s performance and financial position. He explained the key sections of an annual report, including the income statement, cash flow statement, balance sheet, notes to the financial statements, auditor’s report, events after the reporting period and Environmental, Social and Governance disclosures. He also shared practical insights on how financial information can be interpreted and used to better evaluate a company’s overall financial health. The Institute actively supports financial literacy initiatives and contributes to related national efforts through its participation in the Malta Financial Services Advisory Council Financial Literacy Working Group.

The MIA Networking Event welcomed more than 700 members and professionals from across the accountancy and business community for an evening of networking, celebration and connection. The event marked a significant milestone for the Institute with the official unveiling of the MIA's new brand identity and logo, reflecting a renewed vision for the future of the profession. Beyond bringing the profession together, the event also demonstrated the generosity and community spirit of MIA members. Through registrations, over €7,000 was raised in support of The Malta Trust Foundation, with all proceeds being donated to help further the Foundation's valuable work and initiatives. The Institute extends its sincere appreciation to all attendees, sponsors including Scope, KPMG, Deloitte, PwC, EY, RSM, Jesmond Mizzi Financial Advisors and Fyorin, and contributors whose participation helped ensure the success of the event, making it both a memorable celebration and a meaningful opportunity to give back to the community.

Ahead of the summer months, the MIA team stepped away from their daily routines to enjoy a team-building lunch, providing an opportunity to connect, reflect and celebrate collective achievements. It was a welcome opportunity to recharge, foster collaboration and reinforce the positive culture that continues to drive the MIA forward. At the heart of the event was a simple reminder that strong teams are built not only through professional collaboration, but also through shared experiences and meaningful connections.
MIA Rebranding: A New Identity for a Dynamic Profession 26 June 2026

The Malta Institute of Accountants has unveiled its new brand identity, marking an important milestone in the Institute's continued evolution. More than a visual refresh, the new identity reflects the MIA's vision for the future and its ongoing commitment to professional excellence, innovation and the development of both its members and the wider business community. The new brand embodies a modern and forward-looking profession, while remaining rooted in the values that have guided the Institute throughout its journey. It serves as a symbol of the MIA's dedication to supporting its members, fostering growth and responding to the changing needs of the profession in a dynamic environment. As the Institute looks ahead, its new identity will continue to represent a profession that is progressive, resilient and ready to embrace new opportunities.
Inspiring Future Finance Professionals at the I Choose Fair 24 July 2026

The MIA participated in this year’s I Choose Fair, engaging with students and promoting the wide range of opportunities available within the accountancy and finance profession. A key highlight of the event was the panel discussion “Careers in Finance: Your Journey Towards Unlimited Opportunities,” which brought together MIA members Annette Gauci, Gabriella Borg and Andreas Lanzon to share insights into their professional journeys and discuss the evolving role of finance professionals in today’s business environment. The discussion emphasised how accountancy extends far beyond numbers, with professionals contributing to strategic decision-making, business growth, innovation, governance and value creation across a diverse range of industries. Throughout the fair, the MIA was also supported by representatives from leading accountancy firms, including Deloitte, KPMG, PwC, RSM and BDO. Together, they welcomed students at the MIA stand, where young people had the opportunity to learn more about the profession, ask questions about their future studies and career prospects and gain a better understanding of the many pathways available within accountancy and finance. The Institute’s presence at the fair forms part of its ongoing commitment to raising awareness of the profession among younger generations and providing aspiring professionals with the information and guidance needed to make informed decisions about their future careers.

MIA Assistant Technical Managers Kristina Busuttil and Laura Farrugia attended The Malta Tax and Customs Administration (MTCA) Stakeholders Forum 2026. The event brought together stakeholders to review the organisation’s performance over the past year and discuss key priorities for the future. It commenced with an opening address by Commissioner Joseph Caruana, who outlined the forum's objectives and the strategic direction for the year ahead. This was followed by a presentation of the Annual Report 2025, highlighting major achievements, performance results, strategic initiatives and key milestones reached during the year. A significant part of the forum focused on upcoming legislative and operational developments affecting stakeholders. Discussions covered important topics including Value Added Tax in the Digital Age, domestic e-invoicing and Digital Reporting Requirements, Flat-Rate Duty and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Participants were also provided with an update on the Integrated Tax and Customs Administration System project, including its objectives, implementation progress, expected benefits for taxpayers and practitioners and the planned rollout.
Interview on Business News Malta 10 August 2026

The MIA CEO was invited by the Malta Financial Services Authority to participate in an interview for its Boardroom Brief series, which was published on the Business News Malta platform. The interview explored the evolving role of the accountancy profession in a rapidly changing regulatory and technological environment, covering topics such as the impact of the new EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority, the growing influence of artificial intelligence on the profession, talent attraction and skills shortages and the MIA's ongoing contribution to policy development and professional education. The discussion also highlighted the Institute's role in supporting members, promoting proportional and effective regulation and strengthening Malta's competitiveness and resilience.

During the first half of 2026, the MIA continued strengthening its connection with the profession through a series of member outreach visits to audit and accountancy firms across Malta. These visits provided a valuable opportunity to engage directly with members, gain insight into the challenges and opportunities facing the profession and ensure that the Institute's initiatives remain aligned with the needs of practitioners. Such engagements play an important role in helping the MIA remain informed, responsive and member-focused. To date, visits have been carried out at Agius & Associates, Advitac, CutajarBusuttil Accounting, JP Audit & Advisory Services Limited, Borg Galea Associates, 3a Malta, Tri-Mer Services Malta and Nouv. The Institute looks forward to continuing these engagements in the months ahead as part of its ongoing commitment to supporting and representing the profession.

The European Commission (EC) has published a package of proposed tax measures that could reshape key aspects of cross-border taxation within the European Union (EU). Released on 24 June 2026, the taxation omnibus package introduces amendments to several major EU tax Directives, including the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the Parent-Subsidiary Directive and the Interest and Royalties Directive. Among the proposed changes are updates to interest limitation rules, the treatment of Pillar Two entities under controlled foreign company rules and the removal of certain holding requirements, reflecting positions that have been discussed at European level in recent years. In parallel, the Commission has proposed a recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC), bringing together the various DAC regimes within a single legislative framework. The proposal seeks to simplify reporting requirements, reduce administrative burdens and enhance the effectiveness of information exchange between tax authorities. Key measures include adjustments to DAC6 and DAC7 reporting obligations, the introduction of a unified notification mechanism for certain reporting frameworks and the development of a centralised EU Tax Identification Number verification system. The proposals are expected to form part of ongoing discussions on the future direction of tax cooperation and compliance across the European Union.
EC Releases Two DAs Under ESG Ratings Regulation

The European Commission (EC) has adopted two Delegated Acts supporting the Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Ratings Regulation. The measures further clarify the supervisory responsibilities of the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA). The first Delegated Act establishes the enforcement framework, including the procedures ESMA will follow when conducting investigations and imposing fines or periodic penalty payments. The second introduces a fee regime for ESG rating providers, setting different charges for entities established within and outside the EU. Both Delegated Acts remain subject to scrutiny by the European Parliament and the Council before entering into force.

The European Commission has adopted revised sustainability reporting standards designed to reduce compliance costs and administrative burdens for businesses, while maintaining the quality and usefulness of sustainability disclosures. The package also introduces a voluntary reporting framework for smaller companies, offering a proportionate approach to sustainability reporting and information requests throughout value chains.
EC Sets Detailed Application Requirements for ESG Rating Providers

The EC has adopted technical standards setting out the information and documentation requirements for ESG rating providers seeking authorisation or recognition in the EU. The standards establish a more structured and consistent application process, helping to ensure that ESMA receives the information needed to assess applicants effectively. The measures form part of the broader ESG Ratings Regulation framework aimed at enhancing transparency, reliability and supervisory oversight of ESG rating activities.
EFRAG Launches Interactive Hub for Revised ESRS and Voluntary Standard

EFRAG has launched an interactive hub bringing together the 2026 Revised European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and the Voluntary Standard, with the aim of helping stakeholders navigate and apply the updated requirements more effectively. The resource includes comparison tools, amendment logs and links to previous ESRS versions, with additional supporting materials expected to be added over time.

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Malta’s long-term credit rating at ‘A+’ with a stable outlook, highlighting strong economic growth, high income levels and European Union (EU) membership. The agency said Malta remains among the best-performing economies it rates, with the economy expanding by 90% since 2015, compared with 16% across the euro area. Average annual growth stood at 6.5% over the period. Fitch also welcomed Malta’s improving fiscal position and falling deficit, but warned that governance standards have deteriorated over the past decade, posing a key challenge to the country’s credit profile.
MFSA publishes Financial Crime Compliance Strategy

The Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) has published its Financial Crime Compliance Strategy 2026, outlining a forward-looking supervisory framework aimed at strengthening Malta’s approach to combating financial crime. The strategy focuses on risk-based and outcomes-driven supervision, ensuring resources are directed towards higher-risk sectors and activities while promoting effective compliance. The strategy also supports Malta’s preparation for significant European developments, including the implementation of the EU’s anti-money laundering package and the establishment of the Anti-Money Laundering Authority.
New pay transparency rules enter into force

Employers in Malta will face stronger obligations on pay transparency following the transposition of the EU Pay Transparency Directive into Maltese law through the Equal Pay (Transparency and Reporting) Regulations, Legal Notice 173 of 2026. The new regulations reinforce the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value between men and women, introducing clearer requirements on pay transparency, more formal reporting obligations and stronger enforcement mechanisms. Employers will be expected to have clear, evidence-based systems in place to assess pay practices and address potential inequalities, placing greater emphasis on transparency and accountability in the workplace.

Malta’s economic growth is expected to remain robust, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast to expand by 3.8% in 2026, 3.6% in 2027 and 3.8% in 2028, according to the forecast published by the Central Bank of Malta. Private consumption is expected to remain the main driver, with the 2026 growth projection revised slightly upwards. Inflation is projected to ease to 2.2% in 2026, from 2.4% in 2025, before rising slightly in 2027 amid geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions in the Middle East. The budget deficit is projected at 2.2% of GDP in 2026 and is expected to narrow to 1.6% by 2028, while debt is forecast to fall to 44.2% of GDP. The Bank said that risks remain broadly balanced, although prolonged Middle East tensions could weigh on activity and increase inflationary pressures. Higher services inflation and increased energy support spending also pose risks.
BDO Malta has announced the appointment of Andrea Kis as Audit Director with effect from January 2026.
RSM Malta has announced the appointment of Ludwig Micallef as Director with effect from 24 August 2026.
Grant Thornton Malta has announced the appointment of Brunella Bugeja as Senior Manager – Indirect Tax, with effect from 8 July 2026.
EY Malta has announced the appointment of Silvio Camilleri and Chris Bugeja as Partners with effect from July 2026.

PwC Malta has announced the appointment of David Micallef as Head of Business Unit (HBU) within PwC Digital Services effective from 1 July 2026. He will be leading the firm's Cloud and Infrastructure and IT Managed Services team.

The Malta Tax and Customs Administration (MTCA) and the Department of Accountancy, within the University of Malta’s Faculty of Economics, Management and Accountancy, are pleased to announce the launch of a new workshop series for Master in Accountancy students. The first workshop, to be held in December 2026, represents a collaborative effort to provide Master in Accountancy students with hands-on experience of the tax process, return submission and practical online submission problem solving. In collaboration with the Department of Accountancy, these workshops will be run by MTCA’s newly formed Education Section, which forms part of the Strategy & Innovation Division within MTCA. Through increased investment in education and public awareness, the MTCA new section is committed to building stronger connections with the community and recognises the importance of fostering an informed and responsible tax knowledgeable society. The workshop initiative is expected to further strengthen the division's efforts, creating valuable opportunities for learning while promoting a greater understanding of the role taxes play in supporting society. Through these initiatives and partnerships, MTCA is investing in a more informed, responsible and financially aware society, helping to empower future generations with the knowledge and values needed to contribute positively to Malta’s continued development and prosperity.

Quality Assurance (QA) is an important element of the audit profession. In an environment shaped by evolving standards, increasing stakeholder expectations and heightened regulatory scrutiny, organisations cannot treat audit quality as a periodic compliance exercise. It must operate as an integrated, risk-focused and forward-looking framework that supports public trust, strengthens accountability and drives continuous improvement. The shift from quality control to quality management is particularly significant for the profession. International Standard on Quality Management 1 requires firms to design a system of quality management that is tailored to their nature and circumstances and based on a proactive assessment of quality risks. This reflects a broader regulatory expectation: quality should be embedded in governance, culture, methodology, monitoring and remediation, rather than addressed only after deficiencies arise.
The Role of Quality Assurance in Today’s Professional Environment

At its core, quality assurance provides confidence that professional work is performed consistently, competently and in accordance with applicable standards, laws and ethical requirements. It serves several interconnected purposes: protecting the public interest, helping firms and practices identify weaknesses before they develop into systemic issues and providing findings that highlight whether a firm's policies, procedures and behaviours are operating effectively in practice. Effective quality assurance also reinforces professional scepticism, ethical conduct and accountability. It helps ensure that teams do not simply complete the required steps but understand the purpose of those steps and apply judgement appropriately. In this sense, quality assurance is not merely a review function; it is a mechanism for learning, improving and sustaining trust.
Challenges Facing QA Functions in a Rapidly Changing Landscape

Quality assurance functions are facing a wider and more complex set of challenges than in the past. Standards and regulatory requirements are evolving, particularly in areas such as quality management, sustainability reporting and assurance, ethics, anti-money laundering, technology and data governance. At the same time, firms and practices must respond to increasing market pressure, talent shortages, fee constraints and growing expectations from clients, investors, regulators and the public. Another challenge is the pace of technological change. Digital tools, automation, analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) can improve efficiency and insight, but they also introduce risks relating to data quality, security and over-reliance on automated outputs. QA teams must therefore develop the ability to evaluate not only traditional engagement files and processes, but also the controls surrounding technology-enabled work.
Regulatory and Supervisory Drivers for Stronger QA Frameworks

Regulators and oversight bodies continue to place strong emphasis on the design and operation of quality management systems. Inspection programmes across jurisdictions have highlighted recurring deficiencies in audit execution, documentation, risk assessment, professional judgement and internal monitoring. In Europe, supervisory convergence, sustainability assurance, technological innovation and cross-border oversight are also shaping the regulatory agenda. Competent authorities are increasingly focused not only on whether organisations have documented policies, but whether those policies are effectively implemented, monitored and improved.
Modernising QA Frameworks for Effectiveness and Efficiency

Modern QA frameworks should be designed around effectiveness, proportionality and efficiency. This means moving away from static checklists and towards systems that focus on the areas of greatest risk and impact. Technology can support this shift. Over recent years, the profession has devoted considerable attention to the potential of AI to transform audit. Some firms and practices, primarily coming from a network, have started using AI tools in a number of areas to assist them in the audit process. It is envisaged that the use of AI will continue to become more and more significant in the coming years. In addition, the Quality Assurance Unit (QAU) has started developing artificial intelligence tools to support the performance of its own inspections, and discussions are ongoing at the Committee of European Auditing Oversight Bodies (CEAOB) on the future use of AI in supervisory activities. Although using AI tools in quality assurance frameworks can assist in facilitating the work carried out, technology should enhance professional judgement, not replace it. The most effective frameworks combine digital capability with experienced review, clear accountability and timely dialogue with those responsible for quality. Another important aspect brought more into the spotlight by the International Standard on Quality Management 1, is that findings should be analysed for root causes, translated into practical improvements and monitored to determine whether corrective actions are effective. Without this cycle, quality assurance risks becoming an exercise in reporting deficiencies rather than resolving them.
Embedding Risk-Based Thinking in QA Processes

A risk-based approach is central to a credible QA framework. It requires both firms and regulators to identify where quality risks are most likely to arise and where their consequences would be most significant. This may include complex or high-risk engagements, new service lines, significant regulatory changes, inexperienced teams, independence threats, tight reporting deadlines, recurring inspection findings or areas involving substantial judgement. Risk-based thinking should influence the scope, timing and depth of QA activities. Higher-risk areas may warrant more frequent monitoring. Lower-risk areas should not be ignored, but the level of work should remain proportionate. The purpose is not to reduce scrutiny, but to direct attention where it is most needed.
Strengthening Competence and Capacity in QA Teams

The effectiveness of the Quality Assurance function ultimately depends on the quality assurance reviewers carrying out the reviews. QA reviewers need not only technical expertise, but also the ability to challenge constructively, identify root causes, communicate findings clearly and influence behavioural change within firms and practices. They should understand standards and regulation, but also the practical realities of how work is performed. In addition to undertaking continued professional education, reviewers within the QAU are given opportunities to participate in training activities organised within the CEAOB to keep abreast of new developments at European Union level. Within the QAU, over the past year, additional staff members have been engaged and are undergoing on-the-job training to strengthen their competencies in quality assurance. This investment in capacity is essential to ensure that reviews remain robust, proportionate and responsive to emerging risks.
Practical Recommendations for Firms and Practices

Firms and practices seeking to strengthen their QA frameworks should begin with a clear assessment of whether the framework remains fit for purpose. This includes evaluating governance responsibilities, documented policies, monitoring activities, reporting lines, escalation processes, remediation procedures and the quality of management information provided to leadership. Cold file reviews should be viewed as an important tool for improving the quality of future audit work, rather than as a narrow compliance exercise. Reviewers should have the necessary competence, independence and practical experience to assess files thoroughly, challenge appropriately and identify both individual deficiencies and wider patterns of non-compliance. The outcome of such reviews should provide meaningful insight into whether audit methodology, supervision, review procedures and documentation are operating effectively in practice.

In a changing regulatory landscape, quality assurance frameworks must be proactive, proportionate and resilient. The firms and practices that will be best placed to respond are those that treat quality as a strategic priority, embed risk-based thinking into their processes, invest in competent teams and use monitoring outcomes to drive continuous improvement. Strong QA frameworks do more than satisfy regulatory expectations; they protect trust, strengthen professional performance and support the long-term credibility of the profession.

Where findings are identified, firms and practices should evaluate their severity, recurrence and underlying causes. Remedial actions should be specific, proportionate, time-bound and assigned to accountable owners. Root cause analysis should be embedded as a standard discipline, particularly for significant or recurring deficiencies, so that actions address the reason why issues arose rather than only correcting the immediate file-level matter. Finally, firms and practices should ensure that lessons learned from monitoring activities are fed back into training, methodology updates, consultation processes and leadership discussions. A quality assurance framework is most effective when it creates a continuous improvement cycle: identifying risks, reviewing performance, addressing deficiencies, monitoring remediation and reinforcing a culture in which audit quality is consistently prioritised.

authors.bio: Ms. Karen Sultana is the Head of the Accountancy Board's Quality Assurance Unit within the Ministry for Finance. She is a certified public accountant and holds a practising certificate in auditing with the Accountancy Board. She is also a fellow of the Malta Institute of Accountants. Since 2006, she has been actively involved in quality assurance and assists the Board in regulatory matters.

body: The ecosystem of Transfer Pricing (TP) revolves around the arm’s length principle. In simple terms, the objective is to ensure that intra-group transactions are priced in accordance with the prices at which independent enterprises operating under similar economic, market and business conditions but without any control or influence over one another, transact or would have transacted. While this may sound simplistic, the application of the arm’s length principle comes with its own nuances and complexities. As a discipline, TP aims to approximate business reality. Accordingly, any TP analysis undertaken without a clear understanding of the underlying business, its value drivers and how the transacting parties fit within the broader value chain, is inherently flawed. It is for this reason that getting a thorough understanding and analysing the functions performed, assets employed and risks assumed (FAR) by the transacting parties takes centre stage in determining the arm’s length amount. Following the accurate delineation of the transaction, the FAR analysis feeds directly into the comparability analysis by facilitating the identification and selection of appropriate comparables. Accordingly, it serves as the foundation upon which the arm's length nature of the transaction is determined. Put simply, a FAR analysis seeks to identify the economic substance of the transaction and, therefore, constitutes a core component in accurately delineating the transaction from a TP perspective.

As recognised in paragraph 1.42 of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Transfer Pricing Guidelines, 2022, a FAR analysis should begin after reviewing the written contractual terms reflecting the intentions of the parties at the time of entering into the transaction and governing the transaction, including the documented roles and responsibilities of the transacting parties. However, a written contract is merely the starting point and should not be relied upon exclusively for determining the arm’s length nature of a transaction. Indeed, the objective of a FAR analysis is to test contractual allocation against the actual conduct of the parties, particularly which entity exercises control over the risk, has the financial capacity to assume it and bears the economic consequences of that risk.

A proper FAR analysis should seek to identify and break down the economically significant FAR in relation to the transaction and appropriately assign them to the transacting parties. Further, one-sided TP methods such as the Cost-Plus Method, Resale Price Method and the Transactional Net Margin Method, require the selection of a tested party. Simply put, the tested party is generally the entity with the least complex FAR profile and for which reliable comparable financial information is available. It is therefore the entity whose contribution is easier to value. Accordingly, documenting the FAR profile of each transacting party becomes essential to identifying the tested party. To put this into perspective, below follows a FAR analysis for a transaction wherein the tested party, say Company A, performs routine software development functions for Company B, which acts as the economic entrepreneur within the MNE. Ideally an explanation of each parameter would also be provided, but this is omitted for the sake of brevity.

A FAR analysis should be conducted in a manner that identifies the actual economic reality of the transaction. While there is no prescribed roadmap, most TP experts recognise that the best approach to adopt is as follows:

Before analysing any transaction, it is important to understand the business, its drivers and how the transaction fits within the overall business model. Each and every transaction typically has an objective. Relevant information may be gathered from stakeholders, industry sources, the Multinational Enterprise’s (MNE) Master File and its website(s).

Once the contractual terms and business are understood, functional interviews should ideally be conducted with key stakeholders directly involved in the transaction. The objective is to identify and assign economically significant FAR to each transacting party. This may be supplemented through questionnaires or checklists.

The overall strategy formulation within the MNE was undertaken by Company B in its capacity as the MNE’s economic entrepreneur and key decision-maker. Key managerial personnel engaged by Company B were responsible for driving the MNE’s strategic objectives. The transaction under consideration did not involve any core strategic functions, and Company A’s role was limited to executing the service based on the directions and framework established by Company B.

The decision-making and strategy formulation in relation to end third-party pricing were driven by Company B. In the context of the transaction under consideration, the pricing was determined mutually between Company A and Company B by applying an arm’s length mark-up on the total operating costs incurred by Company A in providing the said services.

Company B was responsible for the formulation and monitoring of the MNE’s global marketing strategies and campaigns. The MNE’s Chief Marketing Officer was also engaged by Company B. Company A did not perform any marketing functions given that it operated as a captive software development service provider within the MNE and its only customer was Company B.

The overall quality control parameters were formulated by Company B in accordance with the directions of the Chief Operating Officer engaged by Company B. Company A, in its capacity as a captive service provider, was expected to adhere to these quality control parameters in relation to the services provided.

Routine tangible assets in the nature of office infrastructure were employed by Company A in providing the services. Such infrastructure primarily included leased office premises, furniture and computer equipment.

The key intangible assets of the MNE, namely the unified customer services platform and the relevant brand, were legally as well as economically owned (explained below) by Company B. The key personnel engaged by Company B were responsible for performing the strategic development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation functions in relation to these intangible assets. Company A neither owned nor employed any such intangible assets. Its role was limited to providing routine services to Company B.

Factors such as the availability of substitutes, entry of new players or competitors reducing the prices of comparable products could adversely impact market share. Company B, being the MNE’s economic entrepreneur, assumed and controlled market risk decisions, including pricing and strategy, and had the financial capacity to bear potential losses. Company A, being a captive service provider with no direct market-facing exposure, was not directly exposed to this risk. However, any adverse impact on the business of Company B could have indirectly affected the demand for services rendered by Company A.

Operational risk primarily relates to disruptions to business activities arising from operational breakdowns or poor financial health/performance. Company B was primarily exposed to this risk, as it was responsible for ensuring the operational and financial health of the MNE under the directions of the Chief Operating Officer and the Chief Financial Officer. Company A was also exposed to this risk, albeit to a limited extent, given that it was assured of a fixed mark-up over its total operating costs and operated within the operational parameters established by Company B.

Credit risk primarily relates to the risk of non/late repayment of outstanding dues. Company B, being exposed to end third-party customers, primarily assumed the credit risk. Company A was exposed to this risk only to a limited extent in the context of the services rendered. However, given that its customer was Company B, the intensity of this risk was minimal. During the period under consideration, invoices raised by Company A were settled by Company B within 60 days in accordance with the intercompany agreement.

Forex risk primarily relates to the risk of impact of forex currency fluctuations on the profitability of the Company. Company B raised invoices on third-party customers primarily in USD, whereas its reporting currency was Euro. Accordingly, Company B was exposed to foreign exchange risk. However, this risk was partially offset by expenses incurred in USD. In the context of the services provided by Company A to Company B, Company A raised invoices in Euro, which was also its reporting currency. Accordingly, Company A was not exposed to any foreign exchange risk. This can be summarised as follows:
Routine development, limited pricing inputs, basic quality control.
Group Strategy, strategic marketing, pricing, setting quality control parameters.

Having regard to the FAR profiles of Company A and Company B, Company A was concluded to be the least complex entity and the one for which the most reliable comparable data was available. It was therefore selected as the tested party, given that its profile was akin to a routine software development support service provider. Company B, on the other hand, was characterised as the economic entrepreneur engaged in strategic and non-routine functions within the MNE.
How frequently should a FAR analysis be refreshed?

Typically, a FAR analysis should be reviewed annually and updated where there are material changes. Think of it from this perspective: in Year 1, a transaction is priced based on the intentions and actual conduct of the transacting parties at that point in time. But what if, in Year 2, the circumstances are no longer the same? What if the parties perform functions that they did not perform in Year 1, or there is a significant change in their risk or asset profile? Such changes could invalidate the pricing strategy originally adopted for the transaction. While the intensity of the exercise may not be as high where the fact pattern remains substantially unchanged, proceeding with the assumption that nothing has changed could potentially lead to non-arm’s length outcomes.

A thoroughly documented and well-substantiated FAR analysis lies at the heart of any TP analysis. Conducting a robust FAR analysis is essential to accurately delineate the transaction under consideration and evaluate the actual conduct of the parties against their contractually documented roles and responsibilities, if any. The high degree of subjectivity involved in TP makes it more of an “economist’s art” than an exact science. Consequently, global TP litigation today is at record levels, with a significant proportion of disputes centered around the accurate delineation of the controlled transaction.

A comprehensive FAR analysis embedded in timely contemporaneous documentation thereof therefore plays a pivotal role in enabling taxpayers to demonstrate adherence to the arm’s length principle and also serve as the first line of defense in the event of scrutiny by tax authorities.
