body: Professional judgement has always been at the heart of the accountancy profession. Whether in financial reporting, auditing, assurance or emerging areas such as sustainability, standards alone cannot anticipate every situation, nor provide a predetermined answer to all technical questions. Economic reality evolves faster than regulatory frameworks, and business models are increasingly complex. In this context, professional judgement is not simply desirable; it is indispensable. However, the environment in which that judgement is exercised is in a constant state of change. At European Union (EU) level, supervisory expectations are converging, enforcement activity is becoming more coordinated and stakeholders are demanding greater transparency and comparability. As a result, professional judgement is exercised under ever greater scrutiny, creating a structural tension between flexibility and consistency. This is not a marginal issue. It speaks to how the profession can keep serving the public interest as regulation becomes more complex in practice.
The Growing Convergence of Supervisory Expectations

Over the past decades, the EU has made significant progress in strengthening the coherence of its regulatory and supervisory frameworks. Bodies such as the European Securities and Markets Authority, the European Banking Authority and, in the area of reporting, EFRAG, previously referred to as the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group, play an influential role in shaping expectations on interpretation, disclosure and enforcement. This convergence reflects a broader objective: reinforcing trust in the Single Market. Investors, lenders and other stakeholders rely on financial and non-financial information to allocate capital efficiently across borders. For this to function, they must be able to interpret information consistently, regardless of where it originates. Supervisory convergence contributes to this goal. Through common enforcement priorities, coordinated reviews and ongoing dialogue between authorities, it reduces fragmentation and improves the overall robustness of reporting practices. Yet, it is important to distinguish convergence of expectations from similar application of requirements and supervision in all circumstances or uniformity of outcomes. While regulators may align on principles, entities operate in different economic, legal and organisational environments. It is therefore inevitable, and often appropriate, that similar principles lead to different conclusions in different, especially national, contexts. The objective of European convergence should not be to eliminate judgement, but to ensure that judgement is exercised consistently in terms of process, quality and transparency.
Consistency Across Jurisdictions: A Persistent Challenge

Despite progress in regulatory coordination, achieving consistent application of EU law, regulation and standards across jurisdictions remains a major challenge. Inconsistency rarely stems from disagreement on the wording of standards. Instead, it arises in areas such as:

Materiality is definitely a case in point. It is inherently entity-specific and context-dependent, requiring qualitative and quantitative judgement. Two professionals may reach different conclusions based on similar facts, and both conclusions may be defensible. The challenge emerges when such differences are perceived as arbitrariness rather than reasoned outcomes. This challenge is even more pronounced in emerging fields such as sustainability reporting. Concepts like double materiality, transition risk assessment and value chain analysis involve significant estimation and forward-looking assumptions. Practices are still evolving, and interpretative frameworks are not yet fully stabilised. For multinational groups, the complexity is compounded by cross-border operations. Centralised reporting processes must accommodate diverse regulatory expectations and supervisory cultures. Judgements acceptable in one jurisdiction may be challenged in another. In such a scenario, increasing the volume of rules is unlikely to be the solution. More detailed requirements may reduce some ambiguity, but they often generate additional complexity and unintended rigidity. Consistency is better achieved through stronger judgement discipline: clear reasoning, robust documentation and transparent communication of assumptions and limitations.
Principles-Based Frameworks and Enforcement: A Necessary Tension

A defining feature of European reporting frameworks is their principles-based nature. This is a deliberate design choice. Principles-based standards allow professionals to reflect economic substance rather than merely comply with formal rules. They provide the flexibility needed to adapt to innovation and changing business environments. However, principles-based frameworks interact with increasingly detailed enforcement practices. Regulators, understandably, seek assurance that standards are applied rigorously and consistently. Over time, enforcement decisions, thematic reviews and public communications may create a body of expectations that can appear more prescriptive than the standards themselves. This creates a delicate balance. If enforcement becomes overly prescriptive, there is a risk that professionals shift from exercising judgement to managing compliance risk. Judgement is not eliminated but replaced by risk-averse behaviour. In such a scenario, the focus may move from faithfully representing economic reality to anticipating regulatory preferences. This dynamic can have unintended consequences. Reporting may become more extensive but less informative. Disclosures may increase in volume while decreasing in clarity and relevance. Assurance processes may become more compliance-oriented rather than judgement-oriented. Effective enforcement should therefore focus on the quality of judgement rather than its outcomes. The distinction between weak judgement and well-reasoned judgement leading to a different conclusion is fundamental. A mature supervisory ecosystem recognises that consistency does not require identical answers; it requires credible, transparent and defensible reasoning.

One of the central challenges of modern reporting is balancing flexibility with comparability. Flexibility is necessary because entities differ in their business models, strategies and risk profiles. Reporting must reflect these differences to provide meaningful information. Comparability is equally important, as users need to assess performance and risks across entities and jurisdictions. This tension is particularly evident in non-financial reporting. While financial reporting benefits from established conventions and decades of practice, sustainability reporting is still developing. It often involves forward-looking information, uncertain data and evolving metrics. In this context, comparability cannot rely solely on standardised indicators. It requires transparency about methodologies, assumptions and limitations. High-quality reporting is not only about what is disclosed, but about how clearly it explains the underlying reasoning. This is where professional judgement creates value: by bridging the gap between standard requirements and economic reality. The objective is not to eliminate differences, but to ensure that differences are understandable, justified and transparent.
The Role of Professional Bodies and Standard Setters

Professional bodies and standard setters play a critical role in maintaining and enhancing the quality of professional judgement. Their contribution extends beyond technical rulemaking. They provide guidance, education, ethical frameworks and platforms for dialogue between practitioners, regulators and policymakers. In periods of significant regulatory change, such as the ongoing development of EU sustainability reporting and assurance, this role increases in relevance. Professionals now need support not only in understanding standards, but in applying them in practice. This includes methodologies, examples, interpretative guidance and opportunities to share experience across jurisdictions. Professional bodies act as a bridge between high-level principles and operational reality. They help translate regulatory expectations into practical approaches while preserving the flexibility necessary for judgement. Equally important is the reinforcement of ethical foundations. Professional judgement is not purely technical. It combines technical competence with integrity, professional scepticism and a clear sense of responsibility towards the public interest. Standard setters contribute by designing frameworks that encourage thoughtful application rather than mechanical compliance. Standards that clearly articulate objectives while avoiding excessive prescription are more conducive to robust judgement. Finally, continuous professional development is essential. The scope of judgement is expanding beyond traditional financial reporting to include areas such as sustainability, data governance, digitalisation and emerging technologies. The profession’s skill set must evolve accordingly.
From Framework to Practice: Strengthening Trust in Judgement

Ultimately, the future of professional judgement in Europe will be defined by the profession’s ability to maintain trust in a more complex environment. Trust no longer depends solely on compliance with standards, but on the quality of judgement processes. This includes:
• technical understanding of the objectives behind standards
• robust internal governance and challenge mechanisms
• clear documentation of reasoning and assumptions

Professional judgement is not only about technical competence but also about the willingness to act on it with integrity and, where necessary, moral courage. Moreover, constructive dialogue across the regulatory ecosystem is essential. Regulators, standard setters, professional bodies and practitioners all contribute to improving outcomes when engagement is collaborative rather than adversarial. Professional judgement should not be seen as a weakness in principles-based systems. On the contrary, it is their defining strength, provided it is exercised rigorously and responsibly.

As EU-level scrutiny continues to increase, the objective should not be to replace judgement with uniformity. Instead, the focus should be on strengthening the credibility and transparency of judgement so that flexibility and consistency can coexist. In a regulatory environment which is becoming progressively more complex, the ultimate goal is not mechanical alignment, but defensible, high-quality decision-making that serves the public interest. That is how frameworks are translated into practice, and how the profession continues to create trust and value.
notes: This content was prepared with human oversight and may have been supported by artificial intelligence tools.

authors.bio: Giancarlo Attolini is an accountant and auditor in public practice in Italy and a founding partner of ASZ, a member firm of the Moore Global network. He has held senior roles with IFAC, EFRAG, the IAASB and IESBA consultative groups, and Italian standard-setting bodies. Since 2025, he has served as Deputy President of Accountancy Europe and was recognised as an IFAC Global Ambassador in 2016.

body: In a complex regulatory and business environment, documentation can no longer be treated as a retrospective administrative exercise. Good documentation is not simply about keeping records or producing evidence when requested. At its best, it is the visible expression of sound governance: it shows how decisions were made, what information was relied upon, who was involved, which risks were considered and whether the organisation acted with appropriate discipline, consistency and accountability. This matters because boards, regulators, auditors and other stakeholders increasingly expect organisations to demonstrate not only that they complied with rules and procedures, but also that they had a defensible basis for the decisions taken. In practice, this requires reliable data, effective controls, clear audit trails and a culture that values evidence-based judgement. In my role as Group Chief Internal Auditor at Mizzi Organisation, I have had the opportunity, and corresponding challenge, to work across a broad portfolio of business interests and industry sectors. Among the many lessons learnt over the years, that diversity has reinforced one key message: governance cannot be effective unless it is supported by reliable information. Whether the matter relates to financial reporting, operational efficiency, regulatory compliance, health and safety, sustainability, procurement, customer service or internal investigations, management and boards need data they can trust. Without reliable data, oversight becomes reactive, controls become difficult to assess and decision-making becomes more exposed to challenge.
Reliable Data Is Therefore Not Merely a Technical Requirement; It Is a Governance Asset.
Reliable Data as the Foundation of Oversight

Good governance depends on timely, accurate and complete information. If data is fragmented, inconsistent, incomplete or poorly controlled, even well-intentioned decisions may be weakened. This is particularly true in diversified organisations, where information may be produced across different departments, systems and operating units. Different teams may define key metrics differently; manual spreadsheets may evolve outside formal control environments; approvals may sit in emails rather than structured workflows; and supporting evidence may be retained inconsistently. Internal Audit has an important role in helping management address these risks. The function should not be viewed only as checking whether procedures were followed. Its value lies in assessing whether governance, risk management and control arrangements are sufficiently robust to support reliable decision-making. This often means asking direct but constructive questions: is the data complete? Is it accurate? Has it been reconciled? Who owns it? Who reviews it? Are exceptions investigated? Is there evidence to support the conclusion? Would the organisation be able to explain and defend this decision if challenged months or years later?

There is a significant difference between having records and having evidence. Records may show that an activity took place; evidence should demonstrate that the activity was properly considered, authorised, reviewed and aligned with the organisation’s policies and obligations. A signed form may confirm approval, but it may not explain the basis for that approval. A management report may show performance against target, but it may not evidence how the underlying figures were compiled or validated. A policy may exist, but it may not prove that it has been consistently applied. This distinction becomes critical when organisations face regulatory scrutiny, external audit, litigation, complaint investigations, whistleblowing reports or internal reviews. In such circumstances, the issue is rarely limited to whether a document exists. The more important question is whether the organisation can demonstrate a coherent, consistent and defensible process. In my experience, some of the most valuable audit and advisory work arises when organisations move beyond asking “Do we have documentation?” and start asking “Would this documentation withstand independent scrutiny?” That shift encourages management to consider whether responsibilities are clear, decisions are traceable, exceptions are justified and evidence is retained in a reliable and accessible manner.
Consistency of Controls Across the Organisation

For diversified organisations, one recurring governance challenge is consistency. Different business units may operate in different sectors, with different systems, customer expectations, regulatory touchpoints and operational pressures. Some local adaptation is necessary. However, excessive variation in control practices can create risk, especially where the organisation expects group-level assurance over compliance, reporting, conduct or risk management. Consistency does not mean uniformity in every detail. It means establishing minimum control expectations while allowing operational teams to implement them practically. Evidence may be captured differently from one business unit to another, but the underlying principles should remain consistent: clear ownership, documented review, appropriate approval, segregation of duties, exception monitoring and reliable retention of supporting information. Internal Audit can support this by identifying good practice across the organisation and helping management understand where controls vary unnecessarily. Advisory work is particularly valuable here. By engaging early on new processes, system implementations, policy development or organisational change, Internal Audit can help ensure that controls and audit trails are designed properly from the outset. It is far more effective to build control discipline into a process at the design stage than to reconstruct evidence after a problem has emerged.

Technology and data analytics are ever more important in strengthening assurance activities. Internal Audit functions can now analyse larger populations of data, identify anomalies, test control effectiveness more efficiently and provide deeper insights to management. Used well, analytics can move assurance away from limited sample-based testing towards more continuous and risk-focused monitoring. This is consistent with the continued evolution of the profession. The Institute of Internal Auditors’ 2024 Global Internal Audit Standards, a mandatory component of the International Professional Practices Framework and with which all internal audit functions are expected to be in conformance, place significant emphasis on the quality, consistency and evidencing of internal audit activities, providing a framework for evaluating and enhancing the performance of internal audit functions. The domains covering the governance, management and performance of internal audit services reinforce an important point: Internal Audit must not only provide assurance but also be able to demonstrate that its work is appropriately planned, performed, supervised and documented, with sufficient evidence to support sound professional judgement and reliable conclusions. At the same time, Internal Audit is entering a new phase shaped by artificial intelligence (AI). Agentic AI tools are being developed and adopted by internal audit teams across the globe. These technologies have the potential to transform the delivery of internal audit activities by supporting and accelerating work across the audit lifecycle, including audit planning, risk assessment, fieldwork, reporting and follow-up. The opportunity is significant, but so is the responsibility. The “human in the loop” remains essential at key stages involving risk assessment, interpretation of results, validation of exceptions, formulation of findings and communication with management and the board. AI can enhance the auditor’s capability, but it should not replace professional scepticism, ethical judgement or accountability. More importantly, the primary challenge in adopting AI within Internal Audit is not simply the technology itself. It is data readiness. AI tools are only as effective as the data they are permitted to access, interpret and rely upon. If organisational data is incomplete, inconsistent, poorly structured, inadequately governed or unsupported by reliable audit trails, the output of even the most advanced tools may be flawed, misleading or difficult to defend.

My experience as Group Whistleblowing Reporting Officer has also reinforced the importance of documentation, evidence and audit readiness. Internal investigations, whistleblowing matters and risk reviews require objectivity, confidentiality and professional scepticism. They also require a disciplined approach to evidence. Conclusions must be supported by facts, not assumptions. Recommendations must be proportionate. Management actions must be traceable. Sensitive matters must be handled with integrity and care. Weak documentation can significantly undermine an organisation’s position. If decisions were made informally, approvals were not retained, responsibilities were unclear or exceptions were tolerated without explanation, it becomes more difficult to establish what happened and why. This does not necessarily mean that misconduct occurred or that management acted improperly; however, weak evidence creates uncertainty and uncertainty undermines confidence. Strong documentation protects the organisation, but it also protects individuals who acted properly. It provides clarity, reduces ambiguity and supports fair outcomes. When evidence is reliable, investigations can focus on facts rather than speculation. When audit trails are complete, management can respond with confidence. When controls are consistent, lessons learned can be translated into practical improvements rather than isolated reactions.
Building a Culture of Audit Readiness

Audit readiness should not be treated as an event shortly before an audit, inspection or regulatory review. It should be a continuous discipline embedded into day-to-day operations. An organisation is audit-ready when people understand their responsibilities, controls operate consistently, evidence is retained naturally as part of the process and management can explain not only what was done but why it was done. This requires tone from the top, but also commitment throughout the organisation. Boards and senior management must set expectations for integrity, transparency and accountability. Middle management must translate those expectations into practical routines. Employees must understand that documentation and controls are not obstacles to performance, but safeguards that support sustainable performance. Internal Audit contributes by providing independent assurance, but also by engaging constructively with management, sharing insights, challenging assumptions and highlighting emerging risks. The most effective Internal Audit functions are respected not because they find issues, but because they help the organisation become stronger, more resilient and better governed.
Conclusion: Defensibility as a Governance Principle

In today’s environment, organisations must be prepared to justify their decisions, evidence their controls and demonstrate that governance is operating in practice, not merely on paper. Documentation, data and audit trails are no longer back-office administrative matters. They are central to trust, accountability and regulatory confidence. From my professional experience, the organisations best placed to respond to scrutiny are not necessarily those with the most documentation. They are those with the right documentation: evidence that is reliable, relevant, accessible and capable of demonstrating sound judgement. Looking ahead, this will become even more important as Internal Audit embraces AI-enabled tools and more advanced forms of assurance. The future of the profession will be more data-driven, more technology-enabled and supported by intelligent automation. Yet the ability to benefit from that future will depend on the quality, integrity and readiness of the data available today. Ultimately, defensibility is not about preparing for criticism. It is about embedding discipline into governance. It is about ensuring that when decisions are challenged, the organisation can respond with confidence, clarity and integrity. In a complex regulatory environment – and in an AI-enabled future – that may be one of the most important indicators of effective governance.
notes: The following primary or official sources were consulted for professional framing and alignment with recognised internal audit, internal control, data analytics and AI audit guidance:
• The Institute of Internal Auditors; 2024 Global Internal Audit Standards; https://www.theiia.org/en/standards/2024-standards/global-internal-audit-standards/.
• The Institute of Internal Auditors; The IIA’s Artificial Intelligence Auditing Framework; https://www.theiia.org/en/content/ tools/professional/2023/the-iias-updated-ai-auditing-framework/.
• Committee of Sponsoring Organisations of the Treadway Commission (COSO); Internal Control – Integrated Framework; https://www.coso.org/guidance-on-ic.

authors.bio: Giancarlo Millo is the Group Chief Internal Auditor at Mizzi Organisation, which operates across diverse industries. He has also been appointed as the Group’s Whistleblowing Reporting Officer and as Chairperson of the Group's ESG Steering Committee. He is a CPA and CIA, holding CISA and CRISC certifications as well as MBA (Fin) and Dip IoD qualifications. Mr Millo presently serves as Chairperson of the Institute of Internal Auditors – Malta Chapter.

body: Online Deposit Platforms (ODPs) are transforming European retail banking by removing geographic barriers, allowing smaller credit institutions to access cross-border liquidity without physical branches. However, ODPs convert granular retail savings into rate-sensitive, highly volatile balances resembling short-term wholesale funding, challenging standard microprudential runoff assumptions under stress. Additionally, layered structures like fiduciary omnibus accounts obscure depositor visibility, fragment compliance responsibilities and elevate financial crime risks. To address these risks, European regulators must move from entity-centric supervision to an activity-based paradigm. This requires platform-specific stress testing, real-time transparency into pooled accounts and binding compliance standards across the intermediation chain.

Digitalisation is reshaping European retail banking as ODPs, or "comparison-plus" platforms, replace traditional, branch-based deposit gathering with cross-border, single-interface access. While ODPs offer institutions, particularly in smaller jurisdictions like Malta, cost-effective funding diversification and enhanced consumer choice, they also challenge longstanding prudential assumptions. By eliminating switching barriers, ODPs transform historically "sticky" retail deposits into highly elastic, mobile capital, exposing underlying differences between direct intermediation and fiduciary or omnibus account structures. Consequently, this article argues that the growth of ODPs necessitates a shift toward activity-based supervision, evaluating funding risks by their economic substance and behavioural dynamics rather than their formal legal classification alone. In line with this argument, the article first examines the limitations of traditional entity-based regulation and outlines the rationale for an activity-based supervisory framework rooted in the principle of "same activity, same risk, same regulation." It then analyses how digital distribution accelerates depositor mobility and discusses how institutions should incorporate platform-specific stress scenarios into their Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP). Next, the article explores the operational, compliance and anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) risks inherent in multi-intermediary and omnibus account structures, focusing particularly on the need for look through capabilities. Finally, it concludes by summarising the key supervisory implications and advocating for prudential oversight that reflects the operational realities of modern digital banking.

European banking regulation pursues microprudential institution-level stability and macroprudential systemic resilience primarily through an entity-based model that applies regulatory requirements to licensed credit institutions. This traditional approach relies on the implicit premise that core banking activities, including deposit mobilisation, occur directly within these regulated entities. However, the rise of ODPs disrupts this assumption. While ODPs operate under non-bank regulatory frameworks and do not conduct unauthorised banking business, they exert a profound influence over funding flows, depositor behaviour and liquidity dynamics. This divergence highlights a structural challenge in modern financial regulation; i.e. identical risks now manifest across varying organisational and technological structures under disparate supervisory regimes. Embracing the regulatory principle of "same activity, same risk, same regulation" requires shifting supervisory focus toward underlying economic functions rather than institutional legal forms. Rather than subjecting ODPs to full bank licensing requirements, an activity-based approach ensures that economically equivalent risks receive consistent, proportionate supervisory scrutiny regardless of the technological architecture used to mobilise deposits.
Benefits and Emerging Risks: the Behavioural Shift in Retail Funding

ODPs deliver significant commercial efficiencies by lowering distribution costs, broadening consumer access and fostering cross-border competition. For smaller institutions operating in constrained domestic markets, these platforms provide a vital mechanism to diversify funding sources without incurring the capital expenditure of physical branch networks. However, the exact mechanisms that drive these efficiencies also alter the fundamental behaviour of the underlying retail deposits. Historically, retail deposits were treated as stable, "sticky" funding due to high switching friction, geographic limitations and search costs. By enabling real-time interest rate comparison and seamless digital transfers, ODPs eliminate these operational barriers, rendering platform sourced deposits significantly more elastic and price sensitive. As demonstrated by the 2023 banking turmoil, including the rapid failure of Silicon Valley Bank, digital connectivity drastically compresses withdrawal timelines. While legally classified as retail funding, these deposits behave with a speed and volatility that traditional prudential assumptions do not fully anticipate. Consequently, liquidity risk assessments must evolve beyond static legal definitions to evaluate empirical behavioural dynamics, focusing on the velocity and triggers of digital capital flows. Rather than altering baseline Pillar 1 liquidity rules, banks with material ODP exposure should address these risks within Pillar 2 through their ILAAP. Supervisors should require tailored stress scenarios that model accelerated run rates, rate-sensitive deposit flight, operational disruptions and digitally driven herd behaviour.

Beyond liquidity risk, ODPs introduce operational, governance and compliance complexities. Platform architectures typically involve multiple intermediaries, including software providers, partner banks and fiduciary agents. In fiduciary or omnibus "for benefit of" structures, deposits are pooled under a single nominee account, effectively severing the direct relationship between the product bank and the end-depositor and obscuring visibility over ultimate beneficial owners. This intermediation creates AML/CFT vulnerabilities. When customer onboarding, sanctions screening and ongoing transaction monitoring are split across multiple entities in different jurisdictions, compliance data becomes fragmented. Despite delegating execution to third parties, product banks retain ultimate legal responsibility for AML/CFT compliance, making clear contractual allocations of duty and real-time information-sharing mechanisms essential to prevent oversights. Furthermore, heavy reliance on ODPs introduces concentration risks and third-party operational dependencies that standard liquidity metrics miss. Disruptions from cyber events, vendor disputes or platform business model shifts can instantly halt deposit intake or trigger rapid outflows. To mitigate these risks, supervisors increasingly demand that institutions establish robust "look-through" capabilities over omnibus accounts, strengthen third-party risk management frameworks and enforce rigorous governance over all platform operations.

ODPs represent a structural evolution in European retail banking, driving market integration and enabling financial institutions to efficiently diversify their funding bases cross-border. However, ODPs are far more than a neutral distribution mechanism; their digital architecture fundamentally alters retail depositor behaviour, increases funding velocity and introduces operational and AML/CFT vulnerabilities. Because these risks stem from the economic and behavioural dynamics of digital intermediation rather than the underlying legal form of the deposits, effective oversight demands an equally modern supervisory response. Rather than stifling innovation through rigid Pillar 1 reclassifications, supervisors should focus on enhancing internal risk management frameworks. This requires incorporating behavioural liquidity analysis, platform-specific ILAAP stress testing, robust look-through capabilities for omnibus structures and strict third-party governance into regular supervisory reviews. Ultimately, the rise of ODPs reinforces the need for an activity-based supervisory paradigm, one that evaluates financial risks by their true economic substance and operational realities, thereby safeguarding stability while preserving the benefits of digital innovation.

body: The past few years have provided many reminders that compliance failures rarely happen because rules do not exist. More often, they occur when frameworks are not properly understood, responsibilities are unclear or risks are not fully integrated into decision-making. From cyber incidents and operational disruptions to challenges around sustainability disclosures and financial crime controls, organisations have seen that good governance depends on how effectively principles are applied in practice.

Bridging that gap between regulation and implementation requires more than technical expertise. It requires judgement, challenge and the ability to see risk as part of business strategy. Sharon Cilia Tortell brings this perspective from a career spanning audit, regulation, consultancy and executive leadership. Today she works with boards and executive leadership on governance, enterprise risk, sustainability and regulatory strategy across the financial services sector.

Alongside her professional roles, she lectures at the University of Malta, is undertaking doctoral research in artificial intelligence (AI) and risk management, contributes to the Malta Institute of Accountants through its respective Insurance and Digitalisation Groups and serves on the Board of the Federation of European Risk Management Associations. This combination of practical experience, research and professional engagement has shaped her view that governance should not be treated as a separate compliance exercise, but as a fundamental part of how organisations make decisions.
“Effective governance is about much more than regulatory compliance,” she begins.
“Its purpose extends beyond protecting organisations; it supports better decision-making, strengthens resilience and creates confidence among boards, regulators, investors, customers and society.”

Compliance is sometimes criticised for becoming a box-ticking exercise, particularly when organisations focus more on demonstrating that controls exist rather than understanding their purpose. For Ms Cilia Tortell, this happens when compliance is viewed as the responsibility of one department rather than a shared organisational responsibility. A strong compliance culture starts with leadership, she adds, with boards and senior management setting the tone through their actions. Employees are more likely to embrace compliance when they understand how it protects customers, supports sound decisions and contributes to long-term resilience. Policies and training also have a role to play. Rather than simply listing requirements, organisations should explain the reasoning behind controls and encourage discussion around practical situations. “A mature compliance culture encourages people to ask questions, challenge decisions and raise concerns early. The objective should not simply be following rules but applying sound judgement.”

Ms Cilia Tortell believes that each stage of her career has added a different dimension to her understanding of risk. Her time in financial services regulation provided insight into supervisory expectations, while consultancy offered exposure to organisations with varying levels of governance maturity. Internal audit strengthened her appreciation of independent assurance and constructive challenge, while risk management reinforced the importance of anticipating potential issues rather than simply reacting once problems emerge.
This broad perspective has shaped her approach today, where she sees governance, risk and compliance as contributors to organisational performance rather than barriers to business activity.

One of the main challenges facing organisations is ensuring that new requirements do not become isolated compliance projects. She is keen to point out that areas such as operational resilience, sustainability reporting, artificial intelligence, financial crime and cyber risk often overlap, yet organisations can sometimes address them through separate initiatives.
“The real task is translating regulatory principles into practical policies, processes, controls and behaviours that employees understand and apply consistently,” she says.

The challenge, she explains, is finding the right balance between meeting regulatory expectations and maintaining proportionality. Organisations need robust frameworks, but they must also avoid creating unnecessary bureaucracy that slows decision-making or limits innovation. Leadership has an important role in achieving this balance. She argues that boards and senior management must communicate not only what regulations require, but also why they matter.

As regulatory frameworks become more principles-based, professional judgement assumes more importance. Regulations cannot anticipate every possible scenario, meaning professionals often need to balance technical requirements with ethical considerations, commercial realities and stakeholder expectations. In this context, she explains that confidence comes from understanding the purpose behind regulation rather than simply memorising requirements. “Exposure to audit, regulation, finance, consultancy, risk management and compliance provides valuable perspectives that strengthen professional judgement. Throughout my own career, one lesson has remained constant: regulations and technologies will continue to evolve, but integrity, independence and sound professional judgement will always remain the qualities that define trusted advisers.”
The Second Line as a Business Partner

The role of the second line of defence has also changed, with risk and compliance functions expected to provide more than oversight. Ms Cilia Tortell believes the second line should be viewed as a partner to the business rather than simply a monitoring function. While independent challenge remains essential, its broader purpose is to help management understand risks before decisions are taken. This includes supporting discussions around risk appetite, challenging assumptions and ensuring governance arrangements remain aligned with organisational objectives. “The second line should help organisations make better decisions, not simply identify problems after decisions have been made,” she explains. Its success, she adds, should not be measured only by the number of findings identified, but by the contribution it makes to resilience, informed decision-making and sustainable outcomes. Technology is another area where governance professionals are facing new challenges and opportunities. Artificial intelligence, in particular, is expected to have a significant impact on risk and compliance functions. Ms Cilia Tortell believes AI can support regulatory monitoring, risk assessment, reporting and horizon scanning, allowing organisations to identify issues earlier and analyse information more effectively. However, she stresses that technological adoption must be accompanied by appropriate governance. Questions around transparency, accountability, explainability, bias and data management will require careful consideration. “Technology should not replace professional judgement. It should provide better information that enables boards and management to make more informed decisions.”

Looking ahead, Ms Cilia Tortell believes that the future of governance and compliance will require professionals with broader skills. Technical accounting knowledge remains essential, but she argues that professionals must also develop an understanding of technology, sustainability, risk management and the wider business environment. Her advice to those building careers in the field is simple: remain curious, continue learning and seek diverse experiences. “A breadth of professional experience provides valuable perspectives that strengthen professional judgement.” While regulations and technologies will continue to change, her message to accountancy and audit professionals remains that the foundations of trusted advice will remain constant. “Frameworks provide the structure, but it is professional judgement that brings them to life. That, ultimately, is what transforms compliance into good governance,” she concludes.
A technical initiative or project I am particularly proud to have contributed to

One initiative is the work carried out on the recent audit exemption changes. The project involved analysing legislative amendments, considering the wider implications for businesses and practitioners and engaging with stakeholders on practical implementation issues. I particularly valued the collaborative nature of the exercise and the opportunity to help develop guidance that supports members in navigating the regulatory changes with greater clarity and confidence.
One aspect of my role that I find especially rewarding

What I find most rewarding is helping technical matters become more accessible and understandable. Whether coordinating with committees, responding to member queries or developing guidance, I enjoy transforming legislation, standards and regulatory requirements into practical insights that professionals can apply confidently in their day-to-day work.
A professional lesson that has shaped the way I approach technical work

One lesson is that technical accuracy and practical relevance must go hand in hand. Even the most technically correct interpretation has limited value if it cannot be applied in practice. I have also learnt the importance of consultation and collaboration, as different perspectives often highlight considerations that might otherwise be overlooked.

body: Scope announces a new partnership with Talexio, bridging payroll and accounting through connected, intuitive cloud solutions.

Businesses increasingly turn to specialist cloud platforms to manage everything from accounting, payroll, HR, and customer relationships. The real value emerges when these systems communicate, allowing information to flow seamlessly between platforms. Building those connections has been central to Scope’s approach for over a decade. The Malta-based cloud specialist works locally and internationally to identify fitting technologies, finding synergies between systems to build leaner ecosystems. Scope’s portfolio now includes Talexio, a Maltese HR, payroll, and time-attendance platform that manages employee records, leave, and workforce processes. Bringing Talexio into Scope’s cloud suite promises a smoother flow of payroll and financial data, less manual work, and better coordination between departments. Scope has built strategic relationships with leading providers including Xero, Zoho, Syft, and Zuper. Rather than locking clients into a single platform, the company brings together complementary technologies. Talexio was a natural fit. “We’ve actually been working with Talexio for a number of years and we’ve always been impressed by their professionalism, their forward-thinking approach and the way they’ve developed solutions around a very specific set of business needs,” explains Brian Ferris, Co-Founder and Head of Strategic Software Solutions at Scope. “We’ve also simply liked working with them as people. We share a similar philosophy of wanting to deliver genuine value for clients, so formalising that relationship felt like a very natural next step.” A key element is Talexio’s integration with Xero. As the official Xero ambassador in EMEA, Scope notes that payroll journal entries can be mapped within Talexio and sent directly to the Xero ledger, retaining the mapping for future runs. Instead of re-entering data by hand, the systems talk directly, cutting manual entry and errors. Neville Micallef, Co-Founder and Head of Tech at Scope, sees this as removing a barrier between systems meant to work together. “We’re always adapting to what our clients need, and we’ve increasingly seen the value in bringing payroll and financial processes closer together,” he says. “By combining payroll capabilities with accounting platforms, we can give clients a much more joined-up process. It’s also an important partnership for Scope as we continue to build our network of trusted technology and industry relationships, much like our work with the Malta Institute of Accountants and Accountancy Europe. These partnerships strengthen our capabilities and expertise, while helping us expand into new areas and build further relationships that can deliver more value for our clients.” The partnership is equally significant for Talexio. Currently serving over 2,000 clients and processing more than 34,500 payslips monthly, Talexio is Malta’s fastest-growing HR and payroll platform, combining local expertise with automation and workforce insights. “At Talexio, our mission has always been to improve organisational well-being with our leading HR, payroll and time attendance platform,” says Mark Camilleri Gambin, CEO at Talexio. “Partnering with a forward-thinking expert like Scope accelerates that vision. Their excellence in cloud strategy, combined with our software and its seamless Xero integration, creates a perfect synergy. Together, we are giving businesses a unified, powerful ecosystem where their workforce and accounting work in perfect harmony.” As Scope expands across Malta, Cyprus, Dubai, and European markets, partnerships like this support its platform-agnostic strategy to deliver connected workflows and less administrative drag. “The more we understand how different platforms can work together, and the opportunities that creates, the more value we can deliver to clients looking to make the most of their cloud investment,” Ferris adds. Micallef sees the Talexio-Xero integration as indicative of Scope’s broader direction. “There are so many platforms available today that fatigue and overwhelm are becoming real problems for businesses, before you even get to the operational headache of making different systems work together,” he says. “That’s exactly why we do this work on our clients’ behalf: researching and testing platforms, finding the best ways to connect them, and making sure those systems work around each business’s specific workflows. The Talexio integration is a good example of what’s possible when we do that, and it’s something we’ll continue to pursue as we work with more clients and expand into new markets.”

Malta's creative sector continues to evolve, with artists, performers, designers, writers and other creative professionals increasingly building sustainable careers through self-employment. While creative practitioners are naturally focused on developing their craft, understanding tax and VAT obligations is equally important to ensure compliance and long-term success.

Whether providing services locally or internationally, creative professionals operating independently may be considered taxable persons for VAT purposes. Understanding the relevant registration requirements and available tax incentives can help avoid unnecessary complications as artistic activities grow.
When does VAT registration become relevant?

Creative practitioners who generate income through artistic or creative activities on a continuous basis are generally considered to be carrying out an economic activity. This can apply to a wide range of professions, including photographers, graphic designers, musicians, dancers, filmmakers, writers and visual artists operating on a self-employed basis.
Depending on annual turnover levels, individuals may be required to register for VAT under either Article 10 or Article 11 of Malta's VAT legislation.

Understanding the different VAT registrations Article 10 registration applies where taxable turnover exceeds the applicable threshold. Registered persons charge VAT on supplies made and may generally recover eligible input VAT incurred on business expenses.
Article 11 registration may be available where turnover remains below the threshold. Registered persons do not charge VAT but are also unable to recover input VAT on business-related costs.
Selecting the correct registration is important, particularly as turnover levels change over time.

For artists and creative practitioners, success extends beyond artistic ability. Understanding the tax and VAT framework applicable to self-employment can provide greater certainty, reduce compliance risks and allow individuals to focus on developing their creative careers with confidence.
Seeking professional guidance can help ensure that the appropriate registrations are in place and available incentives are fully utilised as artistic activities continue to evolve.

Tax incentives available to creative practitioners Malta offers a preferential tax regime for eligible self-employed artists and creative professionals. Subject to meeting the relevant criteria, artistic income may benefit from a reduced tax rate of 7.5% on income up to the prescribed threshold.

The scheme applies to a broad range of artistic disciplines, including musicians, singers, composers, writers, actors, dancers, filmmakers, visual artists and other recognised creative professions, including those practising on a part-time basis.

Social security considerations In addition to income tax and VAT obligations, self-employed creative practitioners are generally required to pay Class 2 Social Security Contributions. These contributions should be factored into financial planning when setting fees and managing artistic activities.
"For creative practitioners, financial compliance is not just an administrative obligation; it forms part of building a sustainable and professional creative practice."
